source.title: Subspace-Aware Sparse Autoencoders for Effective Mechanistic Interpretability

record.tranche_reason: The paper argues that single-direction SAE dictionaries can fragment multidimensional features and reports empirical evidence of such fragmentation in GPT-2 and Mistral-7B, refining the claim that representation units are one-dimensional.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports reconstruction, KL, CE, explained-variance, sparsity, and AutoInterp comparisons. Those results do not directly measure the claim versions and are not recorded as rows. The SAE cluster results in Appendix E are reported by the authors; the earlier atom counts attributed to Engels et al. are cited results and are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper argues, by theory and by measurements on standard SAEs in GPT-2 Small and Mistral-7B, that single-direction SAE latents fragment multidimensional features. That bears on V5 (SAE latents as complete, canonical units) and, weakly, on V6 (features being 1-D). Most of the rest benchmarks the authors' own method (SASA).
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that single-direction SAEs are mismatched to multidimensional features. They argue splitting is both geometrically necessary and the optimum the ℓ1 objective selects. SASA consolidates such a feature into one subspace with polynomial rather than exponential sample complexity. Empirically, SASA reduces absorption and matches standard SAEs on about half the tokens. They note that coordinates inside a subspace are not yet interpretable.
record.recipe_differences: The paper analyzes and compares standard SAEs with a new block-sparse, subspace-aware autoencoder; it does not reproduce the original toy-model method.
record.method_sensitivity: Theoretical bounds depend on intrinsic dimension, co-activation budget, reconstruction error, and regularization. The empirical activation results concern selected GPT-2 layer-7 concept slices; the SAE cluster analysis uses different clustering procedures for GPT-2 and Mistral-7B. The first-letter absorption results vary by model and architecture.
record.problems: Empirical evidence on feature geometry uses selected concepts and two LLMs; the paper reports no uncertainty estimates for these results. The decoder-cluster evidence depends on clustering procedures, and the paper does not test feature stability across seeds or models. The absorption benchmark is not a direct test of canonical feature units.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 KL, CE, explained-variance, and sparsity results were left out because they do not directly measure the listed claim versions. The external standard-SAE atom counts attributed to Engels et al. in Section 7.3 were omitted because they are cited results.

untested.parts: No toy-network sweep of sparsity versus dimension, no phase transition, no geometry of superposed features.
No test of neuron polysemanticity or capacity competition.
No test of other causes of polysemantic neurons.
SAEs are used as a tool. There is no test of whether features are spread across neurons or whether a dictionary recovers real sparse features; Table 1 reconstruction metrics are only SAE quality.
Stability across seeds or runs and canonicality across dictionary sizes or models are not tested.
No direct test separating 1-D from multi-D features in real models beyond a few selected concept groups; the real-model circular features are cited from Engels et al.

missing.what: Synthetic manifolds (circle di=2, sphere and helix di=3, d=64): five standard SAEs split each into 9–171 atoms, vs one SASA group. Also the empirical covering count tracking the Theorem 4 bound.
Mean absorption across standard architectures on GPT-2 layer 7 at the same token budget: ReLU 0.267, JumpReLU 0.553, Gated 0.240, TopK 0.114, BatchTopK 0.192.
Mistral SASA geography group 1570: fires on cities, countries and continents; PCA separates them into clusters.
Sports subspace, SASA group 1056, with three PCA-separated term families.

record.verdict_notes: The record linked V6 rows as 'supports', which is backwards: the study argues against 1-D features. Its real-model dim90 and mixture-of-subspaces evidence shows low dimensionality, not non-1-D features. V4 links are removed throughout. SASA-only rows (r3, r10, r12, r14, r16) are the study's own method. The cluster analyses use different procedures for the two models and report no uncertainty. The Engels et al. atom counts are cited, correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: No toy-model sweep tests a sparsity-dependent transition or regular geometry for sparse features in superposition.
The paper studies SAE latent splitting, not whether neuron polysemanticity arises from capacity competition or whether important features receive dedicated neurons.
No result tests polysemantic neurons or alternative causes of neuron polysemanticity.

The paper tests SAE decoder clusters and selected concept analyses in GPT-2 and Mistral-7B, but not how features are distributed across neurons generally or how broadly SAEs recover features across models and concepts.
The paper reports SAE fragmentation and absorption, but does not test feature stability across seeds or training runs, or establish whether SAE features are canonical across models or methods.

The paper reports multidimensional structure in selected LLM activation slices and SAE groups, but does not establish that all model features are multidimensional or that all superposed features have this geometry.

rows.subject: standard SAE decoder risk (theoretical)
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed the minimum ℓ1-regularized reconstruction risk for a decoder representing a single multidimensional feature slice.
rows.measure: Lower bound on the number of decoder directions needed for uniform approximation
rows.value: L_i^(k)(ε) ≥ C(t/ε)^((di−k)/k); when k ≥ di, an orthonormal basis gives zero error with di directions.
rows.note: Theoretical result for a single-feature slice, not an empirical toy-network result.
rows.check: Theoretical bound, conditional on a feature having di ≥ 2. It assumes multi-D features rather than testing V6, so V6 is removed. Under that assumption, single-direction latents cannot be complete units.

rows.subject: standard SAE decoder risk (theoretical)
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed whether adding and rotating decoder directions lowers the optimal ℓ1-regularized decoder risk.
rows.measure: Risk of the basis dictionary versus a path toward an overcomplete covering dictionary
rows.value: There is a continuous path from the basis dictionary to strictly lower risk; the paper states that optimization favors Θ((t/λ)^(di−1)) near-collinear atoms in the k=1 regime.
rows.note: A theoretical analysis of the specified SAE objective; it is not a reported training-run measurement.
rows.check: Theoretical landscape result, conditional on di ≥ 2: the ℓ1 objective prefers split, near-collinear atoms. It does not test whether features are multi-D, so V6 is removed. No training-run measurement.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.2, Theorem 8 and the following discussion.

rows.subject: SASA objective (theoretical)
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed global minimizers of the Top-1 block-sparse SASA objective on a single-feature slice.
rows.measure: Number of active blocks and recovered feature subspace
rows.value: Every global minimizer activates a single block whose decoder recovers Vi; the paper states uniqueness up to block index and orthogonal rotation.
rows.note: This concerns the proposed SASA objective, rather than an empirical test of standard SAE units.
rows.check: Theory about the study's own SASA objective. It does not measure standard SAE units or real model features.

rows.subject: GPT-2 Small
rows.operation_detail: Applied PCA to raw activations on controlled temporal concept prompts and reported the dimension capturing 90% variance.
rows.measure: dim90, the number of principal components capturing 90% variance
rows.note: The result concerns a selected temporal activation slice, not all features.
rows.check: dim90=14 is for a slice pooling days, months, years and seasons. Several 1-D features would also give dim>1, so the measure cannot separate 1-D from multi-D features. The record's 'observed' and 'supports' had the direction wrong for V6.

rows.subject: GPT-2 Small
rows.operation_detail: Applied PCA to raw activations on controlled geography concept prompts and reported the dimension capturing 90% variance.
rows.measure: dim90, the number of principal components capturing 90% variance
rows.locator: Appendix D, Figure 4b and accompanying text
rows.note: The result concerns a selected geography activation slice, not all features.
rows.check: dim90=33 pools city, country and continent prompts, so it cannot distinguish many 1-D features from multi-D ones. It shows low dimensionality, not non-1-D features.

rows.subject: GPT-2 Small
rows.operation_detail: Compared held-out reconstruction by a mixture of local subspaces with global PCA on raw activations.

conditions.value: K = 256 clusters, local rank 16, up to 16 selected local subspaces

rows.locator: Appendix D, Figure 5 and accompanying text
rows.note: The authors characterize the raw activations as better described by a mixture of low-dimensional local subspaces than by a single global subspace.
rows.check: Mixture of local rank-16 subspaces (83.95%) vs global PCA rank 256 (74.46%) shows local low-rank structure. It does not test whether individual features are 1-D.

rows.subject: Mistral-7B-v0.1 standard SAE
rows.operation_detail: Clustered decoder vectors and compared cluster size with PCA dimension needed to capture at least 80% of cluster variance.
rows.locator: Appendix E, Figure 6 and accompanying text
rows.note: The authors interpret the ratio as evidence that features are often split across collinear vectors.
rows.check: Median size/PCA-dim ratio of 1.67, only for clusters larger than 3, built by a 0.5 cosine-graph rule. It is evidence of redundant split atoms, not canonical units. V4 is removed: clustering decoder atoms does not test whether models contain recoverable sparse features.

rows.subject: GPT-2 Small SASA
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed temporal concepts represented by a SASA decoder group and its activation geometry.
rows.value: One group of 6 vectors captures the temporal relations; the paper reports that PCA separates temporal categories and that the learned subspace recovers seasonal cyclic order.
rows.note: The paper's earlier count of 35 standard-SAE atoms for days, months, and years is attributed to Engels et al. and is not included as an independent result.
rows.check: A rank-6 SASA group responds to days, months, years and seasons. This is consistent with a multi-D temporal representation, but one group could hold several 1-D features. The seasonal cycle comes from a ridge map fitted to circle targets, so it is partly imposed. Evidence against V6 is weak. The result comes from the authors' own method, and V4 is removed.
